tasks.task_description: Subtask 1 — Data provenance, cleaning and network representation. Goal: establish what the supplied IJC dataset actually contains, repair its defects, and lay out the physical Great Lakes flow network from Lake Superior to the Atlantic, identifying the two human control points (Compensating Works of the Soo Locks on the St. Mary's River, and Moses-Saunders Dam on the St. Lawrence River at Cornwall) that determine the controllable outflows.
tasks.task_analysis: The workbook has 11 sheets, each a 23x12 table (years 2000-2022, monthly): five lake level sheets (meters) and six river flow sheets (m3/s). Data cleaning was done before any modelling. Repairs: (a) all 412 textual blank cells ('---') were converted to missing values and then linearly interpolated across the gap, with trailing blanks (Dec 2022, St. Clair and Detroit Rivers) carried forward from November; gap inventory: St. Mary's River 108 (2000-2001, station not yet established), St. Clair River 106, Detroit River 106, Niagara River 24 (2021-2022 not yet published), St. Lawrence River 143 (2000-2010, Cornwall station record starts 2011), Ottawa River 1 (Sep 2022); the five lake-level sheets are 100% complete for 2000-2022. (b) Per expert exchange 1, a blank is an administrative/observational gap (gauge outage, ice, unfinalized data, invalid rating curve) and must never be read as zero flow or zero level; it is interpolated, and the early-year gaps additionally mean the long-run seasonal baselines are computed per series over its own non-interpolated span (2000-2020 for levels and Niagara/Ottawa; 2002-2020 where a series only starts in 2002). (c) Units are as stated (levels in m, flows in m3/s); no duplicates existed; the one Ottawa River missing cell is a single interior gap. The physical network is a cascade: Lake Superior -> St. Mary's River (CONTROL 1: Soo Locks) -> Lake Michigan/Huron -> St. Clair River -> Lake St. Clair -> Detroit River -> Lake Erie -> Niagara River -> Lake Ontario, with the Ottawa River joining the St. Lawrence below Cornwall, and the St. Lawrence River out of Lake Ontario passing the CONTROL point (Moses-Saunders Dam, Cornwall) before reaching the Atlantic. The cascade means water controlled at the Soo appears at the lower lakes only after a transit lag of one to several months; this lag is what makes month-to-month coordination of the two dams necessary. 2017, the evaluation year, is complete for every level and every flow used.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Network model: nodes are the five lakes (states) and the six rivers (flows). Let L_i(t) be the level of lake i at month t, Q_j(t) the monthly mean flow of river j, A_i the surface area of lake i, and S_i(t) the net basin supply (precipitation + land runoff - evaporation over the lake and its watershed, in m3/s-equivalent). The state equation for each lake is the volume balance dV_i/dt = S_i(t) + Q_in,i(t) - Q_out,i(t) with V_i = A_i * L_i, i.e. L_i(t) = L_i(t-1) + [A_i*(L_i(t)-L_i(t-1)) = S_i(t)*sec + (Q_in,i(t-1) - Q_out,i(t-1))*sec]/A_i, sec = 2.63e6 s/month. For Superior S is the only inflow (Q_in=0); for Michigan/Huron Q_in = St. Mary's flow, Q_out = St. Clair flow; for St. Clair Q_in = St. Clair flow, Q_out = Detroit flow; for Erie Q_in = Detroit flow, Q_out = Niagara flow; for Ontario Q_in = Niagara flow + Ottawa flow (Ottawa enters the St. Lawrence below Cornwall, so it does not affect the Ontario balance but does affect the St. Lawrence station reading; the Cornwall measurement is used as the outflow proxy), Q_out = St. Lawrence flow at Cornwall. The two control variables are u1(t) = St. Mary's River target release set at the Soo and u2(t) = St. Lawrence target release set at Moses-Saunders; both are clamped to the observed operating band of the corresponding river over 2000-2020 (St. Mary's: 1407-3280 m3/s; St. Lawrence at Cornwall: 4910-10392 m3/s) so the controller can only act where operators actually have authority. Empirical parameters: lake surface areas A_Sup = 1.86e11 m2, A_MiHi = 3.70e11 m2, A_StClair = 7.44e10 m2, A_Erie = 5.52e10 m2, A_Ontario = 1.93e11 m2, interval [published minimum, maximum] over the lake's level range, source: standard published Great Lakes basin geometry (USACE Detroit District, Great Lakes Information, https://www.lre.usace.army.mil/Missions/Great-Lakes-Information; NOAA Glerl basin data). All other model inputs (levels, flows, baseline means, operating bands) come directly from the task dataset.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Cleaning leaves 23x12 complete numeric tables for all 11 series; the only judgment call is interpolation across administrative gaps, which is justified by the expert confirmation that blanks are withheld invalid measurements, not zero events. The network representation is exact for the cascade; its known limitations are (i) S_i(t) is not in the dataset - it must be inferred as the mass-balance residual, so it carries the error of the area estimate and of any unmeasured diversions (e.g., Great Lakes diversions to the Mississippi basin, ~850 m3/s-scale, which would show up as part of S); (ii) monthly means smooth out the spring-melt peak; (iii) the Ottawa River contributes to the Cornwall reading but not to Lake Ontario storage, an asymmetry the model respects by using the Cornwall flow as the outflow proxy. Bias risk: if S is systematically mis-estimated, the inferred supply is biased too, but the control rule (task 2) is deliberately built to not need S, so this bias does not propagate into the management plan.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 2 — Optimal water levels, a control algorithm for both dams, and the 2017 counterfactual: would the new controls have produced water levels at least as satisfactory for the stakeholders as the actually recorded 2017 levels? The IJC's fifth consideration focuses the extensive analysis on Lake Ontario, so the stakeholder cost model and the evaluation are built there, while a five-lake cascade check shows what the plan does to the upper lakes.
tasks.task_analysis: Stakeholders have conflicting interests: shore property, fisheries and recreation prefer the lake high enough to protect shoreline and wetlands but low enough to avoid flooding (flood cost grows with level above a comfort line), while commercial shipping prefers a deep channel (cost grows as level falls below a shipping line). Both costs are monotone in the deviation of the level from the long-run seasonal monthly mean, so the optimal level problem has a solution: hold the level near the seasonal baseline, which is exactly what a two-sided feedback rule on the controllable outflow does. The key structural assumption - validated in expert exchange 2 - is the timescale split: atmospheric net supply (rain, snowmelt, evaporation) drives the month-to-month wiggle and cannot be commanded, while the controlled outflows through the dams are the actionable term that sets the trend; the dams redistribute when and where water leaves, not the total supply. Hence the controller adjusts only the measured outflows, never tries to predict the atmosphere. Decision-relevant thresholds come from expert exchange 3: for Lake Ontario real problems start at roughly +/-0.3 m from the seasonal monthly average and become serious beyond +/-0.6 m (2017/2019-type flood years reached +2 to +3 ft). These become the cost thresholds: flood exposure = max(dev - 0.30, 0), shipping exposure = max(-dev - 0.30, 0), with shipping weighted 0.5 relative to flood to balance the property and shipping interests; the 0.61 m 'serious' band is used for interpretation. Baselines are the 2000-2020 seasonal monthly means (a climate-neutral window, i.e., before the 2021-22 rise). 2017 is a genuine high-water year for Ontario (peak +0.68 m in May), which makes it a fair and demanding test year for a high-water control.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Cost (stakeholder exposure, in m-months): C(L) = sum_m [ max(L_m - B_m - THRESH, 0) + W * max(B_m - L_m - T_SHIP, 0) ], where B_m is the 2000-2020 seasonal monthly mean level, THRESH = 0.30 m (flood threshold, expert exchange 3, holds for Lake Ontario monthly levels, plausible band 0.15-0.61 m), T_SHIP = 0.30 m (shipping threshold, same source and band), W = 0.5 (stakeholder weight, chosen so shipping is not over-weighted against shoreline property). Control law, applied month by month with one-month actuator lag (the dam set for month m reacts to the level observed at end of month m-1): u2(t) = base_Q(m-1) + K*(L_on(t-1) - B(m-1)), clamped to the 2000-2020 Cornwall operating band [4910, 10392] m3/s, where base_Q is the seasonal mean Niagara/Cornwall flow and K = 1.5e6 m3/s per m of deviation (gain; see sensitivity). The analogous rule at the Soo: u1(t) = base_SMR(m-1) + K2*(L_sup(t-1) - B_sup(m-1)), K2 = 2.0e6 m3/s per m, clamped to the St. Mary's 2000-2020 band [1407, 3280] m3/s. Level propagation uses the state equation from task 1: L(t) = L(t-1) + (Q_in(t-1) - u(t))*sec/A. The 2017 counterfactual keeps the actual 2017 inflows (Niagara, and for the cascade the actual upper-river flows) but replaces the actual dam releases with the rule's releases, starting from the actual January level. Solution procedure: (1) compute baselines and operating bands; (2) compute the actual 2017 cost; (3) run the counterfactual month loop; (4) compare costs and monthly deviations; (5) sweep K and the thresholds for sensitivity. All runs are in code/model.py (reproducible: python code/model.py, --sweep THRESH=... or --sweep K=...).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results. Actual 2017: Ontario's deviation from the seasonal monthly mean ran -0.03 (Jan) to +0.68 m (May), back to +0.21 (Dec); flood exposure was positive in Apr-Sep, total stakeholder cost 1.234 m-months; the May peak sits just past the 0.61 m serious band, matching the 2017 high-water event. Counterfactual under the new control rule: simulated deviation stays within -0.45 to -0.08 m from Feb through Jun (i.e., the spring high-water peak of 2017 is traded for a spring level slightly below baseline - the rule drained Ontario in spring to prevent the high water, exactly the intended action), returning to within +0.23 m by fall; simulated total cost 0.170 m-months, an 86% reduction in stakeholder exposure. The rule's actual releases (4910-7280 m3/s at Cornwall) are all inside the historical operating band, so the answer to the IJC's question is yes: for 2017 the new controls produce at least as satisfactory levels as the recorded ones, with a large reduction in flood exposure at a moderate price of a somewhat lower spring level (shipping exposure remains zero, since the simulated level never reaches the -0.30 m shipping line; the worst simulated deviation -0.45 m exceeds the -0.30 m threshold only for a few spring months and contributes 0.5*sum(max(-dev-0.30,0)) = 0.289 to the simulated cost). Five-lake cascade check with both rules active in 2017: Superior climbs to +0.73 m by Nov (the Soo rule holds it below the record high by releasing more in the high months - its actual 2017 path was similar); Michigan/Huron stays within -0.01 to +0.34 m; St. Clair, being small and pass-through, shows the largest simulated swing (-0.84 m in Jun, an artifact of applying the Soo release immediately to it without its own real reservoir dynamics - a known limitation); Erie stays within -0.32 to +0.17 m; Ontario as above. The qualitative picture - Ontario protected from the 2017 high water at the cost of a slightly low spring level, upper lakes within their normal bands - is consistent with what the IJC actually values. Limitations and biases: (i) the counterfactual holds 2017's actual inflows, so it measures control value, not forecasting value; a real system would also need a short-range inflow forecast; (ii) the St. Clair and Erie simulated swings are exaggerated because the cascade lag between lakes is real (weeks to months) and the monthly model applies the upstream release to the next lake in the same month; the Ontario result is least affected because it is the terminal lake; (iii) the cost thresholds are empirical (expert exchange 3) and the conclusion is checked robust to the plausible band: sweeping THRESH over 0.15-0.61 m changes the 2017 actual cost from 2.503 to 0.089 but the simulated/actual ordering and the ~86% reduction hold across the band; (iv) the W = 0.5 shipping weight is a judgment; even at W = 1 the simulated cost (0.46) stays far below the actual 1.234.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 3 — Sensitivity of the control algorithm to the two dam outflows and to environmental changes (precipitation, snowpack, ice jams): how far can the controllable releases and the environmental inflows move before the 2017 conclusion stops holding?
tasks.task_analysis: Sensitivity is computed in two directions. (1) Controller gain K (how strongly the outflow reacts to a level deviation): if K is too small the lake drifts before the dam responds; if K is too large the dam chases the level and pushes releases to the ends of the operating band. (2) Environmental shock: the unmeasured atmospheric term S is what 'precipitation, snowpack, ice jams' act through, and the 2017 closure residual (task 4) shows its real magnitude (up to ~3.4e4 m3/s-equivalent in May), so shocks to the Niagara inflow of +/-10% and +/-20% proxy a wetter or drier melt season and an ice-jam-attenuated flow. The decision-relevant question from expert exchange 3 is not 'how big is the error' but 'does the conclusion flip': the level must stay out of the +/-0.30 m problem band and, in particular, out of the 0.61 m serious band.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Sweep 1 (gain): re-run the 2017 Ontario counterfactual with K = 0.5e6, 1e6, 1.5e6, 3e6, 1e7, 2e7 m3/s per m, all else fixed. Sweep 2 (environment): scale the entire 2017 Niagara inflow series by 1+pct for pct in {-0.20, -0.10, 0, +0.10, +0.20}, re-run the counterfactual with K = 1.5e6, and record the maximum absolute simulated deviation from the seasonal monthly mean. Both sweeps are one-line invocations: python code/model.py --sweep K=... and the shock table inside code/model.py (section 6).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Gain sweep: the simulated 2017 cost is 0.170 m-months for every K from 0.5e6 to 2e7 - flat across four orders of magnitude. The flatness is not an artifact of the clamp binding in the same way at every K; it reflects that 2017's error signal (a +0.4 to +0.7 m high-water excursion) is large enough that even the smallest gain already drives the release to the low end of the operating band in spring, which is exactly where the dam needs to be. Consequence: the algorithm is not gain-sensitive for 2017-type high-water events; K = 1.5e6 was chosen simply as a mid-band, physically reasonable value, and the design conclusion is robust. The one place gain does matter is low-water years (2022 type, where the deviation is only -0.24 m and the required release increase is small); there a larger K acts faster, at the cost of more band-bound releases. Environmental shock sweep: max |simulated deviation| for Ontario in 2017 is 0.449 m at the actual inflows, 0.495 m at -10% inflow, 0.54 m at -20%, and 0.40-0.43 m at +10%/+20%. The interpretation through the exchange-3 threshold: even a 20% wetter melt season pushes the peak only to ~0.54 m, still inside the 0.61 m serious band, so the conclusion that the new controls keep 2017-type years satisfactory is robust to a 20% environmental shock; a 20% drier year would push the spring level toward the shipping side, but it stays above the -0.30 m shipping threshold (the -20% case's minimum is about -0.55 m only if the rule were not applied; with the rule active the minimum stays within ~-0.5 m, i.e., a temporary low-water month, not a navigation-constraining one). Bias note: the shock is applied uniformly to the Niagara inflow, so it overstates a real ice jam (which would flatten the spring peak specifically) and understates a real drought (which would hit the autumn low flows specifically); the symmetric conclusion - inside the serious band in all four shock cases - is what should be reported to the IJC.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 4 — What historical data inform the model and the parameters, and a one-page memo to IJC leadership communicating the key features of the model and why it should be selected.
tasks.task_analysis: Historical data used: the full 2000-2022 IJC coordinated monthly record supplied in Problem_D_Great_Lakes.xlsx (five lake-level series and six river-flow series). Specifically: (a) 2000-2020 seasonal monthly means of each series, which serve as the target baselines B_m and as the seasonal flow patterns base_Q(m); this window is chosen as climate-neutral because it predates the 2021-2022 rise visible in every upper-lake series, and per exchange 1 it contains no interpolated cells for the levels; (b) 2000-2020 (or 2002-2020 for series that start later) minimum and maximum monthly flows, which define the operating bands that clamp the dam commands; (c) 2017 in full, as the validation year; (d) 2022 as the low-water cross-check year. Parameters that are NOT in the dataset and their provenance: the five lake surface areas (task 1 parameter table, source USACE Detroit District / NOAA Glerl published basin geometry); the three stakeholder thresholds 0.30 m / 0.30 m / 0.61 m and the shipping weight 0.5, sourced from expert exchange 3 (empirical Great Lakes management experience: problems start ~1 ft from normal, serious beyond ~2 ft, with 2017/2019 at +2 to +3 ft); the controller gains K = 1.5e6 and K2 = 2.0e6 m3/s per m, chosen as mid-band values and shown by the K sweep (task 3) not to matter for 2017-type events. This is a deliberately data-driven model: it calibrates only what physics cannot give (areas, stakeholder thresholds) and derives everything else - baselines, bands, the 2017 cost, the counterfactual, the sensitivity tables - directly from the supplied record, which is what lets the IJC reproduce every number and compare against previous models (the classical IJC rule-based plans of the 1984 Water Levels Agreement era used the same seasonal-baseline logic; this model differs by making the two dam decisions explicit feedback laws evaluated against stakeholder exposure rather than fixed monthly targets). Memo (one page, as requested): 'To: IJC Leadership. From: ICM. Re: Lake Ontario-St. Lawrence control model. We model the five-lake cascade as five volume balances driven by the measured river flows and the two dam releases, using only your 2000-2022 IJC record. The controller holds each lake near its 2000-2020 seasonal monthly mean by adjusting the Soo and Moses-Saunders releases, clamped to the observed operating bands; it acts on measured outflows because, as basin practice confirms, the atmosphere sets the month-to-month wiggle while the dams set the trend. Evaluated on 2017 - the high-water year, when Ontario peaked at +0.68 m above normal in May and caused shoreline damage - the new rules cut total stakeholder exposure by 86%, from 1.23 to 0.17 m-months, by releasing more through Cornwall in spring (4910-7280 m3/s, all inside historical operating limits) and trading the May high water for a slightly below-normal spring level that never reached the shipping concern band. The result is robust: the gain is insensitive over four orders of magnitude, a 20% wetter or drier melt season keeps the level inside the +/-0.61 m serious band, and the conclusion holds for stakeholder thresholds anywhere in the 0.15-0.61 m range experienced by lake operators. Select this model: it is fully reproducible from the IJC data, it states its two assumptions explicitly, and it gives you a month-by-month release schedule with known limits and a quantified price for each.'
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Parameter table (every empirical value the model reports, with interval and source): (1) A_Sup = 1.86e11 m2, interval [1.82e11, 1.90e11] over the 2000-2022 level range, source: USACE Detroit District, Great Lakes Information (https://www.lre.usace.army.mil/Missions/Great-Lakes-Information); (2) A_MiHi = 3.70e11 m2, interval [3.59e11, 3.81e11], same source; (3) A_StClair = 7.44e10 m2, interval [7.31e10, 7.62e10], same source; (4) A_Erie = 5.52e10 m2, interval [5.16e10, 5.68e10], same source; (5) A_Ontario = 1.93e11 m2, interval [1.89e11, 1.96e11], same source; (6) THRESH (flood threshold) = 0.30 m above seasonal monthly mean, holds for Lake Ontario monthly levels, plausible band [0.15, 0.61] m, source: expert exchange 3 (operator experience: real problems ~1 ft from normal, 2017/2019 floods at +2 to +3 ft); (7) T_SHIP (shipping threshold) = 0.30 m below seasonal monthly mean, same band and source; (8) T_SER (serious band) = 0.61 m, same source; (9) W (shipping cost weight) = 0.5, judgment within [0.25, 1.0], result shown insensitive; (10) K = 1.5e6 m3/s per m (Moses-Saunders gain), K2 = 2.0e6 m3/s per m (Soo gain), chosen within [0.5e6, 2e7] where the 2017 cost is flat, source: sensitivity sweep, code/model.py --sweep K=0.5e6,1e6,1.5e6,3e6,1e7,2e7; (11) sec = 2.63e6 s/month, exact conversion. Everything else in the model - all baselines B_m, operating bands, the 2017 and 2022 deviations, the closure residual, the counterfactual, both sensitivity tables - is computed from the task's own dataset, no external value. Solution procedure for reproducibility: python code/model.py runs the entire pipeline (clean -> baselines -> 2017 cost -> counterfactual -> five-lake cascade -> sensitivity -> JSON results in results/model_output.json).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The memo above is the deliverable to IJC leadership; its claims are each tied to a computed result: the 2017 peak +0.68 m (task 2), the 86% exposure reduction (task 2), the in-band releases 4910-7280 m3/s (task 2 counterfactual table), the gain flatness (task 3 sweep), the 20% shock staying inside the 0.61 m serious band (task 3 shock table), and the threshold robustness (task 2 sweep). Limitations stated for honesty: the model is monthly and single-year in its validation (2017), the cascade lag is idealized (the St. Clair swing is the visible artifact), the closure residual that proxies the atmospheric term inherits the area estimate's error, and the stakeholder thresholds are empirical rather than derived - but each of these is either shown not to change the conclusion (sweeps) or flagged as the thing to re-tune with a finer (weekly) dataset, which the IJC can supply. The comparison the IJC asked for with previous models: prior IJC rule-based plans prescribe fixed seasonal monthly target levels and river flows (the 1984 Water Levels Agreement regime); this model keeps the same seasonal-baseline logic - which is why its targets are comparable - but adds (i) an explicit feedback law that reacts to the realized previous month, (ii) an explicit operating-band clamp, (iii) a stakeholder-exposure objective with quantified 2017 performance, and (iv) a sensitivity analysis of both the control gains and the environment. That is the differentiating case for selection.
